parts.text:
39 Which statement explains why alpha-particles have discrete energies, but beta-particles have a
continuous range of energies?
A
Beta-particles have a much smaller mass than alpha-particles which means beta-particles
can be emitted with a larger range of velocities.
B
Only alpha-particles experience repulsion from the nucleus which is dependent on the
number of protons in the nucleus.
C
Only beta-particles are emitted with another lepton and some energy is transferred to the
other lepton.
D
Only the energy of alpha-particles is discrete because the composition of alpha-particles is
always the same.

hints: Notice the difference in products: alpha-decay gives daughter nucleus plus alpha-particle only, while beta-decay gives daughter plus beta-particle plus another particle.
Recall that total energy released in a given nuclear transition is fixed by the discrete change in nuclear energy, so ask how that fixed energy is divided.
In beta-minus decay identify the other lepton emitted with the electron and consider how variable sharing of energy between the two leptons affects the observed electron energy.
walkthrough: Write the two decays: alpha-decay is $parent \rightarrow daughter + \alpha$, a two-body breakup, while beta-minus decay is $neutron \rightarrow proton + e^- + \bar{\nu}_e$, effectively a three-body breakup including the antineutrino lepton.
For a particular parent to daughter transition the disintegration energy $E$ released is fixed because nuclear energy levels are discrete.

In alpha-decay this fixed $E$ is shared in only one way between the daughter recoil and the alpha-particle by momentum and energy conservation, so every alpha-particle gets essentially the same kinetic energy - a discrete line.

In beta-decay the same fixed $E$ is shared between three products: daughter recoil, beta-particle and antineutrino, and the fraction taken by the antineutrino can vary continuously from near zero to near maximum.
Therefore the beta-particle kinetic energy varies continuously from zero up to a maximum, while the alpha energy does not. This is option C

A.explanation: Mass affects velocity for a given energy but does not create a continuous energy spectrum - the total available energy from the decay is still fixed.

B.explanation: Both alpha-particles and beta-particles are charged and experience electrostatic repulsion from the positively charged nucleus.

C.explanation: Beta-decay emits a beta-particle plus an antineutrino, and the fixed disintegration energy is shared variably between them giving a continuous beta spectrum.

D.explanation: Fixed composition of the alpha-particle does not by itself fix its kinetic energy - the discrete energy follows from two-body decay between fixed nuclear energy levels.
